samples.text:
Nowadays it is very difficult for young people to buy a house because the prices are very high. Some people think the government should improve rented housing instead of helping young people to buy their own homes. I agree with this opinion to some extent.

Firstly, many young people cannot buy a house even with help from the government. They have low salaries at the start of their career and they cannot save enough money for a deposit. If the government give them a small amount of money, the house prices will probably go up and the problem will not be solved. So it is more useful to make rented houses better, because many young people will rent for a long time anyway.

Secondly, the quality of rented houses in many cities is quite bad. Some apartments are old, cold and have problems like damp walls. Also, landlords can increase the rent or ask the tenants to leave with a short notice. This make people feel stressed and they cannot plan their life. If the government make rules to protect tenants and improve the condition of houses, the life of millions of people will become better.

However, owning a home is still a dream for many people. A house gives people security for the future and they don't have to pay rent when they are old. So I think the government should not stop helping completely, for example they can help people who buy their first home with low price.

In conclusion, I mostly agree that the government should focus on the quality and security of rented houses, because this help more people. But some help for young buyers is also necessary.
samples.why: Position mostly clear though slightly hedged in conclusion · relevant ideas, some general · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and article errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
As property prices have risen faster than incomes in many countries, home ownership has become increasingly unattainable for young people. Some argue that governments should therefore concentrate on improving the quality and security of rented housing rather than on helping young people buy homes. I largely agree with this view.

One key reason is that schemes to help first-time buyers often fail to achieve their aims. Grants or subsidised loans increase the amount that buyers can spend, but if the supply of housing does not increase, the main effect is simply to push prices higher. Such schemes also tend to benefit those who were already close to affording a home, while doing little for young people on lower incomes, who may never be able to buy.

By contrast, improving the rental sector would benefit a much larger number of people. In many cities, a growing proportion of young adults rent for most of their twenties and thirties, yet they often live in poorly maintained properties and face sudden rent increases or eviction at short notice. Introducing minimum standards for housing quality, longer tenancy agreements and limits on excessive rent rises would give tenants the stability to settle, start families and plan for the future. In several European countries, where renting is secure and well regulated, it is considered a normal long-term option rather than a temporary stage.

That said, home ownership remains important for financial security, particularly in retirement, when people without property must continue paying rent on a reduced income. Governments should therefore not abandon support for buyers entirely, but it should focus on increasing the overall supply of affordable homes.

In conclusion, I agree that improving rented housing should be the priority, since it would help more young people more quickly and effectively. Support for home ownership should be a secondary goal, achieved mainly through building more homes.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · main ideas extended and supported · clear central topic in each paragraph · range of cohesive devices · some less common vocabulary · mostly accurate with a minor pronoun slip.

samples.text:
In many countries, soaring property prices have put home ownership beyond the reach of a generation of young adults. One response is to argue that governments should prioritise making rented housing better and more secure, rather than trying to help young people onto the property ladder. I agree with this view to a considerable extent, although I believe the two goals are more connected than the statement suggests.

The weakness of many home-ownership schemes lies in their effect on prices. When governments offer deposit grants or subsidised mortgages without increasing the supply of homes, they largely add to demand, and much of the benefit is absorbed by higher prices. These policies also tend to favour those already on the verge of buying, offering little to young people on modest or insecure incomes, and they can be costly for the public purse.

Improving the rental sector, in contrast, would directly benefit the millions of young people who rent, many of them for far longer than previous generations did. Too often they face damp or poorly insulated homes, unpredictable rent increases and the constant possibility of being asked to leave. Enforceable quality standards, longer and more secure tenancies and protection against arbitrary eviction would allow tenants to put down roots, enrol children in local schools and plan their lives with confidence. Where renting is well regulated, as in parts of continental Europe, it is regarded as a respectable long-term choice rather than a precarious stopgap.

Ownership nonetheless matters, not least because retired people who rent must meet housing costs from a reduced income. The most effective way to support it, however, is not through demand-side subsidies but by building more homes, which would also ease pressure on rents.

In conclusion, governments should make secure, decent rented housing their immediate priority, while pursuing wider access to ownership through increasing housing supply rather than through subsidies for individual buyers.
samples.why: Well-reasoned, qualified position fully sustained · ideas extended and logically sequenced · precise, well-managed cohesion · wide, natural vocabulary · wide range of accurate complex structures.
